words.definition: A habitual tendency to tell lies or behave without honesty.
words.example: The witness's mendacity became obvious once phone records contradicted every claim he made.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'men + audacity' — it takes real audacity to lie so freely; from Latin 'mendax,' a liar.

words.definition: To hide your true feelings or intentions behind a false outward show.
words.example: She tried to dissimulate her disappointment, smiling brightly while her hands trembled under the table.
words.mnemonic: Break it as 'diss + simulate' — you simulate a fake self to disguise what you really feel.

words.definition: To describe something falsely or inaccurately, creating a wrong impression.
words.example: The brochure misrepresented the tiny studio as a 'spacious loft with panoramic views.'
words.mnemonic: 'mis-' (wrongly) + 'represent' — to represent something wrongly on purpose.

words.definition: Clever but misleading reasoning used to justify questionable moral choices.
words.example: His defense was pure casuistry, spinning theft into a 'redistribution of resources' with a straight face.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'case-you-istry' — twisting each individual case to suit you; cousin of 'sophistry.'

words.definition: A baseless rumor or false story spread as though it were true.
words.example: The old canard that we use only ten percent of our brains still circulates despite being debunked.
words.mnemonic: French for 'duck' — picture ducks quacking a false rumor across the pond; it's 'hard to swallow.'

words.definition: To damage someone's reputation by making false and harmful statements.
words.example: Rival columnists tried to traduce her, printing invented scandals to ruin her name before the election.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'trash + reduce' — trash-talk that reduces a good reputation to nothing.

words.definition: Pompous, inflated language that sounds grand but carries little real meaning.
words.example: Stripped of its bombast, the CEO's speech promised nothing more than a routine software update.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'bomb + blast' — words exploding with hot air; originally cotton padding stuffed into clothes.

words.definition: To trick someone into believing or accepting something false.
words.example: Con artists duped the elderly couple into wiring their savings to a fake charity.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'dope' — a person who gets duped feels like a dope afterward.

words.definition: To reveal private or secret information to others.
words.example: Bound by contract, the engineer refused to divulge how the encryption actually worked.
words.mnemonic: 'di-' + 'vulgar' (the common crowd) — to make a secret known to everyone, even the vulgar masses.

words.definition: To make previously hidden facts or information known.
words.example: The company was forced to disclose that it had known about the defect for two years.
words.mnemonic: 'dis-' + 'close' — the opposite of keeping something closed; you un-close it to view.

words.definition: Clever trickery or a cunning device used to deceive.
words.example: Her tearful apology was all artifice, staged to win the jury's sympathy.
words.mnemonic: 'art' + 'ifice' — the dark 'art' of crafting a deception; an artful, manufactured trick.

words.definition: A deceptive trick used to conceal something, escape, or reach a goal.
words.example: By subterfuge the spy slipped past the guards, flashing a badge she had forged the night before.
words.mnemonic: 'subter' (secretly, beneath) + 'fuge' (flee) — secretly fleeing beneath everyone's notice.

words.definition: A cunning trick intended to mislead or fool someone.
words.example: Pretending to faint was just a ruse to get the shopkeeper away from the register.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'ooze' — deceit that oozes out; you 'use' a ruse to fool people.

words.definition: A false reason offered to hide the true motive behind an action.
words.example: He visited the office on the pretext of returning a folder, but he came to eavesdrop.
words.mnemonic: 'pre-' + 'text' — the cover story you write out beforehand to explain yourself.

words.definition: An obvious pretense or empty show that convinces no one.
words.example: Their marriage had become a charade, all smiles at parties and silence at home.
words.mnemonic: Think of the party game 'Charades' — a performance acted out, not the real thing.

words.definition: A false or superficial outward appearance that hides the real situation or feelings beneath.
words.example: Behind his cheerful facade, he was quietly struggling with a grief he never mentioned.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'face aid' — the false face you put on to aid in hiding the truth.

words.definition: A thin surface layer that gives a better appearance than what lies underneath.
words.example: Her polite smile was just a veneer stretched over years of deep resentment.
words.mnemonic: A veneer is the thin sheet of nice wood glued onto cheap furniture to look expensive.

words.definition: Something false that is presented as genuine in order to deceive.
words.example: The charity turned out to be a sham that pocketed nearly every donation.
words.mnemonic: Sham sounds like 'shame' — a shameful fake meant to trick you.

words.definition: Made as an exact imitation of something valuable in order to trick people.
words.example: The vendor was arrested for selling counterfeit handbags stitched with fake designer logos.
words.mnemonic: Counter-feit: a fake you'd slip across the 'counter' to pass off as real.

words.definition: A trick that makes people believe something untrue, often as a joke or scam.
words.example: The report of a shark in the swimming pool was a hoax started by bored teenagers.
words.mnemonic: Hoax sounds like 'hocus' (pocus) — a magic trick that fools the whole crowd.

words.definition: Involving deliberate trickery meant to gain money or advantage unlawfully.
words.example: The company collapsed after regulators exposed its fraudulent claims about record profits.
words.mnemonic: Break it down: 'fraud' + 'lent' — money lent out on the basis of a lie.

words.definition: Giving a false or misleading impression that hides the truth.
words.example: The calm surface of the sea was deceptive; a fierce current pulled swimmers out fast.
words.mnemonic: De-CEPT-ive: like 'intercept' — it catches you and traps you in a false belief.

words.definition: Behaving dishonestly by lying or hiding the truth to trick others.
words.example: His deceitful excuses fell apart the moment the receipts were laid on the table.
words.mnemonic: 'Deceit' + full — a person who is simply full of lies.

words.definition: A false belief held firmly despite clear evidence against it.
words.example: He clung to the delusion that the bankrupt firm would somehow make him rich overnight.
words.mnemonic: Delusion sounds like 'illusion' — a false idea that has set up house inside your head.

words.definition: To make someone believe something that is not true.
words.example: Don't delude yourself into thinking one late night of cramming will pass the exam.
words.mnemonic: De-LUDE: it sounds like being 'lured' step by step into believing a lie.

words.definition: To cause someone to have a false idea by giving wrong information.
words.example: The vague nutrition label was designed to mislead shoppers about how much sugar was inside.
words.mnemonic: Mis-lead: to 'lead' someone off in the wrong ('mis') direction.

words.definition: To secretly cooperate in doing something wrong or illegal.
words.example: The guards connived with the smugglers, agreeing to look the other way at the border.
words.mnemonic: Connive sounds like 'con' + 'knives' — cons plotting together with knives in the dark.

words.definition: To work together secretly to cheat or deceive others.
words.example: The two bidders colluded to keep the auction price artificially low and split the savings.
words.mnemonic: Col-LUDE: 'co' (together) + Latin 'ludo' (play) — playing a dishonest game as a team.

words.definition: To plan something harmful or unlawful together in secret.
words.example: The rebels conspired to overthrow the king under the cover of a moonless night.
words.mnemonic: Con-spire: 'con' (with) + 'spire' (breathe) — plotters leaning in to breathe together in secret.

words.definition: A dull, overused remark stated as if it were fresh or meaningful.
words.example: The graduation speech offered nothing but platitudes like 'follow your dreams' and 'never give up.'
words.mnemonic: Platitude sounds like 'flat attitude' — a flat, stale saying with no life left in it.

words.definition: The use of many vague words instead of stating something plainly and directly.
words.example: Rather than admit he was fired, he launched into a circumlocution about 'evolving career synergies.'
words.mnemonic: Latin circum- (around) + loqui (to speak): literally 'speaking around' the point instead of hitting it.

words.definition: Conspicuously and outrageously bad, done openly without any shame.
words.example: The referee whistled a flagrant foul after the player shoved his opponent to the ground.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'fragrant' — a fragrant smell fills the room so everyone notices, and a flagrant act is just as impossible to ignore.

words.definition: Remarkably and shockingly bad in a way that stands out.
words.example: The audit uncovered egregious accounting mistakes that no honest firm could ever have overlooked.
words.mnemonic: From Latin ex grege, 'out of the flock' — it stands out from the herd, for all the wrong reasons.

words.definition: To pretend to have a feeling or condition you do not actually have.
words.example: She feigned surprise at the party, though her sister had spoiled the secret weeks earlier.
words.mnemonic: Feign sounds like 'faint' — a student might feign a faint to get out of a dreaded exam.

words.definition: To hide unpleasant facts or wrongdoing so something appears acceptable.
words.example: The committee's report seemed to whitewash the scandal, pinning the blame on a single junior clerk.
words.mnemonic: Picture painting a filthy, stained wall plain white — you cover the mess rather than actually cleaning it.

words.definition: To formally and solemnly reject or give up a belief, claim, or practice.
words.example: Before the tribunal, the scientist refused to abjure his findings, insisting the evidence was sound.
words.mnemonic: ab- (away) + jure (Latin 'to swear', as in a jury's oath): to swear something away for good.

words.definition: Seeming real but actually false and not to be trusted.
words.example: The startup's promised riches proved illusory once investors examined the empty bank accounts.
words.mnemonic: Shares a root with 'illusion' — like a shimmering oasis in the desert that vanishes the moment you reach for it.

words.definition: A deliberate breaking of trust or faith; treachery toward someone who relies on you.
words.example: His perfidy became clear when the ally he had sworn to protect was quietly handed to the enemy.
words.mnemonic: per- (through/away) + fides (Latin 'faith'): the same fides as in 'fidelity', but with the faith shattered.

words.definition: To make someone appear guilty of a crime or wrongdoing.
words.example: He stayed silent on the stand, unwilling to say anything that might incriminate his brother.
words.mnemonic: in- (onto) + crimen (Latin 'charge, crime'): to lay a crime onto someone's shoulders.

words.definition: Based on false information and therefore not correct.
words.example: The newspaper printed an erroneous figure, claiming the city had ten million residents instead of one.
words.mnemonic: Hidden inside is 'err' — to err is to slip up, so this describes a claim riddled with slip-ups.

words.definition: Using dishonest, indirect, or underhanded methods to get what you want.
words.example: Through a devious web of shell companies, he hid the money from investigators for years.
words.mnemonic: de- (off) + via (Latin 'road'): someone off the straight road, taking a crooked, sneaky path.

words.definition: Willing to act dishonestly, without any moral principles.
words.example: An unscrupulous landlord doubled the rent overnight, ignoring the tenants' signed lease.
words.mnemonic: A 'scruple' is a tiny pang of conscience; slap 'un-' on the front and that conscience is gone entirely.

words.definition: Sounding sweet, smooth, and pleasant to the ear.
words.example: Her mellifluous narration made even the dullest audiobook impossible to switch off.
words.mnemonic: Latin mel (honey) + fluere (to flow): a voice like honey flowing.

words.definition: Moving aimlessly from one thing to another without purpose or enthusiasm.
words.example: He made a few desultory stabs at tidying the room before flopping onto the couch.
words.mnemonic: From Latin desultor, a circus rider who leaps from horse to horse — always jumping around.

words.definition: Happening every day; ordinary and utterly commonplace.
words.example: After a month trekking the Andes, the quotidian grind of emails and dishes felt unbearable.
words.mnemonic: Latin quotidie means 'daily' — think 'quote-a-day,' the same dull thing every morning.

words.definition: Readily able to change form, nature, or appearance; wonderfully versatile.
words.example: A protean performer, she played a weeping widow one night and a slapstick clown the next.
words.mnemonic: Named for Proteus, the Greek sea god who shifted shapes to escape anyone who grabbed him.

words.definition: Too great, beautiful, or intense to be captured in words.
words.example: Standing at the canyon's rim at dawn, she felt an ineffable awe no photograph could hold.
words.mnemonic: in- (not) + eff- (to speak, as in 'effable') + -able: not able to be spoken.

words.definition: Having a thick, sticky consistency that flows slowly.
words.example: The viscous syrup crept down the stack of pancakes, barely seeming to move.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'this custard' — picture thick goo that refuses to pour.

words.definition: Feverish, or marked by hectic, restless nervous energy.
words.example: A febrile excitement gripped the trading floor as the numbers began to spike.
words.mnemonic: Latin febris means 'fever' — febrile is basically 'fever-ile.'

words.definition: Swollen and distended, or pompous and overblown in style.
words.example: The professor's turgid prose buried one simple idea beneath mountains of jargon.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'turbid' and shares a root with 'turgor' — something puffed up and bloated.

words.definition: The region of partial shadow between full light and full darkness.
words.example: During the eclipse we stood in the penumbra, where the sky only half dimmed.
words.mnemonic: Latin paene (almost) + umbra (shadow): 'almost a shadow.'

words.definition: The essential, central part of something; its core substance.
words.example: Skip the anecdotes and just give me the pith of the argument.
words.mnemonic: Picture the soft core running down the center of a plant stem — the heart of the matter.

words.definition: Brisk and cheerful eagerness or promptness in doing something.
words.example: The new intern took on every chore with an alacrity that charmed the whole office.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'a lark' — a lark springs up eager and ready at first light.

words.definition: The power or ability to produce a desired result.
words.example: Clinical trials were designed to test the new vaccine's efficacy against the variant.
words.mnemonic: Shares a root with 'effect' and 'efficient' (Latin efficere, to accomplish) — getting the effect done.
